bp: A journalist covering a social movement is not only asking what people said yesterday. The harder need is to notice when a public conversation is starting to bend because an outside event has changed what people feel, which topics they attach those feelings to, and how loudly those feelings appear. In this paper, the movements are #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter, and the outside event is the 2024 U.S. election. The system, SMART, serves the newsroom task of making reporting more precise and timely around movements connected to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Its raw material is large public discourse: more than 2.7 million Reddit posts and more than 1 million news articles over one year. The practical question is whether a tool can help journalists see shifts in movement discussion early enough to plan coverage, instead of waiting until the shift is already obvious.
wh: The difficulty is that a social movement is not a single number. It is a changing mixture of topics, emotions, events, communities, and media attention. A political event may not merely increase discussion; it may change which themes become emotional, which emotions grow stronger, and whether social media reacts before or after news coverage. Simple volume counts miss this structure. A spike in posts could mean outrage, grief, coordination, backlash, or ordinary attention. Looking only at news articles misses what people are saying in social spaces. Looking only at Reddit misses the external events and public narratives that may be shaping the conversation. The paper also cares about retrospective journalist work, so the system must help connect past discussion to events, not just label isolated posts. The hard part is turning a very large stream of text into event-sensitive, theme-specific emotional evidence without pretending that the extracted emotions are the whole social truth.
naive: A smart beginner might collect posts with movement hashtags, count how many appear each day, and make a timeline around the election. That would be useful as a first dashboard, but it would fail at the main journalistic need. It would show that attention rose or fell, not what kind of feeling changed or which issue inside the movement carried the change. Another beginner approach would be to read a sample of posts after a major event and write a qualitative summary. That keeps nuance, but it is too slow and too small for a year-long collection with millions of posts and articles. The paper's premise is that journalists need both scale and timing: enough evidence to see broad movement patterns, and enough temporal detail to notice shifts while they still matter for editorial planning.
ap: The central move is to treat movement coverage as a pipeline from raw public text to forecastable emotional signals. SMART gathers data from multiple sources, extracts emotions on different themes, and then uses a forecasting engine called DEEP to estimate the future quantity and intensity of emotions in posts. The paper emphasizes retrospective capabilities for journalists, so the tool is not only a prediction box. It is meant to let a journalist look backward across the one-year record, compare discussion before and after the election, and reason about how external events line up with movement discourse. In concrete terms, the system converts many individual pieces of language into time-ordered measurements: how much emotion appears, how intense it is, and which themes carry it. Those measurements then become a basis for detecting discourse shifts early and turning them into actionable newsroom insight.
mech: The mechanism starts with collection. SMART takes in social media discussion and news material from multiple sources; in the demonstrated dataset, that means over 2.7 million Reddit posts and over 1 million news articles across one year. Next, the system identifies movement-relevant material for the case studies on #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter. It then extracts emotions tied to various themes, which means each post is not treated as merely positive or negative in the abstract. The system tries to record what feeling is attached to what part of the movement discussion. Those extracted signals are arranged over time, because the paper's core question is how discourse changes before and after external events such as the 2024 U.S. election. The DEEP forecasting engine then reads the earlier emotional timeline and predicts two future quantities: how many future posts will express emotions, and how intense those emotions will be. The output is a set of time-sensitive indicators that journalists can inspect retrospectively: where the conversation changed, which themes changed, whether the change appears early, and how the movement discussion relates to surrounding news events. The abstract does not describe the interface details or the exact emotion labels, so those parts should be treated as unspecified.
math: The main mathematical ideas are measurement over time, learning from examples, and sequence forecasting. Measurement comes first: many posts are reduced into counts and intensities of emotions on themes. A count answers how often a signal appears; an intensity score answers how strongly it appears. This is a compression step, because millions of documents become a smaller time series that a journalist can scan. The risk is that compression can lose context, sarcasm, disagreement, or minority viewpoints. Forecasting is the next idea. A sequence model looks at earlier points in a timeline and estimates what is likely to come next. The paper says DEEP is transformer-based; in plain terms, that means it can compare many positions in the past sequence and decide which earlier moments are most informative for predicting a later one. The fit is natural because movement discourse has order: events happen, people react, news coverage follows or precedes social discussion, and emotion can build or fade. The tradeoff is timing versus certainty. A forecast can give early warning, but it is only as trustworthy as the emotion extraction, source coverage, and past patterns it learned from.
dots: This paper sits at the crossing of social movement analysis, text mining, time-series forecasting, and information support for human decision makers. It resembles text-mining work because it turns language into structured evidence rather than asking a human to read every document. It resembles social-network and influence work because emotions and movement narratives are not isolated author choices; they reflect events, communities, media attention, and feedback between public discussion and institutions. It also connects to the conference's recurring sequence idea: past events and earlier signals carry information about what may happen next. Compared with a topic-clustering paper such as PRISM in the same batch, SMART is less about discovering narrow topics for their own sake and more about tracking emotional movement around known social issues. Compared with human-AI interface work nearby, it is also a tool paper: its value depends on whether journalists can turn model outputs into better editorial planning rather than just receive another analytic score.
ww: The approach should help because it separates three things that a simple trend chart would mix together: the source of discourse, the theme being discussed, and the emotional shape of that discussion over time. If an election changes public talk around #MeToo or #BlackLivesMatter, the change may show up as a new emotional intensity before it becomes a broad volume spike. A theme-specific emotional timeline gives the system more sensitive evidence than raw counts alone. Multi-source collection also matters because journalists care about the relationship between social movements and external events; news articles and Reddit posts provide different windows into that relationship. The forecasting engine can then use repeated temporal patterns to flag likely near-future shifts. This works only in an intuitive, evidence-based sense described by the abstract: if past emotion sequences contain patterns around events, and if current signals start to resemble the early part of such a pattern, prediction can warn journalists earlier than manual monitoring would.
po: The payoff is an analyst's aid for time-sensitive reporting on social movements. The paper claims SMART enables early detection of discourse shifts around key political events and provides actionable insight for editorial planning. It also contributes a one-year dataset, planned for release, with more than 2.7 million Reddit posts and more than 1 million news articles. The user-centered part matters: SMART was shaped through repeated interaction with more than 20 journalists from varied news organizations over two years. Grounded in the abstract, the gain is not a final theory of #MeToo or #BlackLivesMatter. It is a practical way to connect event timing, movement themes, and emotional changes at a scale journalists could not manually inspect.
limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. Emotion extraction must be accurate enough for movement reporting, but the abstract does not specify the emotion categories, annotation process, error rates, or how sarcasm and contested language are handled. Reddit and news articles are large sources, but they are not the whole public, and their users, editors, and platform norms may skew what appears. Forecasting assumes future discourse partly resembles past temporal patterns; unusual events can break that. The case studies focus on #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter around the 2024 U.S. election, so generality to other movements, countries, languages, or lower-volume issues is not proven here. The tool may guide journalists, but the abstract does not prove that editorial decisions improved in real newsroom deployments.
